hero.title: From Italy to Brazil
paragraphs: A journey of roots, identity, and generations that crossed the ocean.

sections.title: Origins in Italy
paragraphs: With roots in the Veneto region of northern Italy (Castelfranco, Resana, Loreggia), the Perusin family may have even older origins in Umbria (Perugia).
Genealogist Johann Hammer also notes that the family also settled in the Austro-Hungarian regions of 'Küstenland' and 'Istria'.
On the maternal side, the Scoizzato (or Squizzato) family may have origins linked to Switzerland, according to oral history preserved by relatives in Italy and supported by genealogical research.
These movements likely occurred before the 16th century, reflecting early migration patterns in Europe.

sections.title: Perugia: the remote origin of the Perusin?
paragraphs: In 1649, the Jesuit Philip Briet created the map 'L'Umbrie le Perusin le Duche D'Urbin la Marche D'Ancone', part of his work 'Parallela Geographiae Veteris et Novae'.
The map covers the Italian regions of Umbria and Ancona, highlighting the jurisdiction of 'Le Perusin' (Perugia region).
This record is valuable evidence of the origin of the surname Perusin: it arose as an identifier for those born or living in that area, literally meaning 'resident of Perugia'.

sections.title: 4th grandparents, Valentino Perusin and Angela Rossi (Resana, Treviso, 1808)
paragraphs: In this death record of Tomaso and Catterina, dated March 8, 1808, central figures of our lineage appear:
Valentino Bortolleto and Angela Rossi, my 4th grandparents, then 45 and 38 years old, as well as my 5th grandfather, Antonio Bortolleto, who was 71 years old.
In the document, they are identified as the parents and grandfather of the children.

It is worth noting that my Perusin ancestors were called Bortolleto when we lived in Resana-Treviso, to try to differentiate ourselves from other branches of the Perusin family, a common practice of the time.
The suffix '-eto' indicates a diminutive, suggesting that we were descendants of a Bortollo or Bortolomeu, being known as the 'small Bortolemy'.

sections.title: Great-grandparents wedding, Giuseppe Perusin and Lucia Squizzato (Loreggia, Padova, 1884)
paragraphs: On July 13, 1884, in Loreggia (Padua), my great-grandparents Giuseppe Perusin and Lucia Squizzato were married.
This important record also reveals the previous generation, my 3rd grandparents:
Pietro Perusin and Maria Maddalena Bianchi (Giuseppe's parents) and Giovanni Squizzato and Angela Dal Bruoi (Lucia's parents).
Via Sparella 390 was the residence of Giuseppe Perusin and Lucia Squizzato, my great-grandparents, where all their children were born.

A curious fact: when analyzing the records of Giuseppe's uncles and brothers, we can see that the descendants of Valentino Perusin, my 4th grandfather, moved from Resana-Treviso to Loreggia-Padova around 1840 and began to reside in the same location, the old Contrada Via Sparella, changing only the house numbers.

sections.title: Migration to Brazil
paragraphs: In the late 19th century, members of the Perusin and Scoizzato families migrated to Brazil, as part of a broader wave of European immigration.
This movement was driven by economic hardship, land opportunities, and political changes in Europe.

Like many Italian immigrants, they settled in the state of São Paulo, contributing to the development of rural and urban communities. Their legacy became part of the cultural and social fabric of Brazil.

image.caption: About this photo: https://diariodorio.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/08/nave-emigrazione-2.jpg

sections.title: Disembarkation at the Port of Santos (Santos, São Paulo, Brazil, 1897)
paragraphs: My great-grandparents, Giuseppe Perusin and Lucia Squizzato, and their five children, among whom was my grandfather Romeo, left Italy through the port of Genoa on February 1, 1897, and disembarked in Brazil on February 15, 1897, at the port of the city of Santos, in the state of São Paulo.

According to records, they arrived from Italy on the steamship Regina Margherita and then went to the city of Jahú, in the state of São Paulo, to work on the farm of A. Carvalho de Barros. Later, they moved to the city of Agudos.

image.alt: Disembarkation at the Port of Santos
image.caption: Official document of the State of São Paulo.

sections.title: Steamship Regina Margherita: interesting facts
paragraphs: Built in 1884 by the A. McMillan & Son shipyard in Dumbarton, the steamship Regina Margherita was a landmark in Italian shipping.

Commissioned by the Società Italiana Trasporti Marittimi Raggio & C., of Genoa, the ship stood out for its luxury and innovation: it was the first Italian passenger liner equipped with electric lighting.
With a capacity for 1,450 passengers and a crew of 150 people, it offered high-standard accommodations for the time. Even the third class stood out for its excellent ventilation and lighting.

After being launched in 1885, the Regina Margherita inaugurated, in December of that year, regular voyages between Europe and South America, establishing itself as a pioneer of Italian transatlantic routes.

sections.title: São Paulo, Brazil, map
paragraphs: Map of the route followed by my ancestors when they arrived in Brazil in 1897. They left from the port of Santos and headed for Jhaú in the interior of São Paulo. In 1902 they moved to the city of Agudos.
In 1897, the train journey from Santos to Jhaú (present-day Jaú) covered a total distance of approximately 350 kilometers.
The route was not direct, requiring transfers between different railway companies, resulting in a total travel time that could vary between 12 and 15 hours, depending on connections and stops.

image.caption: Illustrative map of the route followed by my Italian ancestors when they disembarked in Brazil through the port of Santos-SP and headed inland in the state of São Paulo, to the cities of Jhaú and Agudos.

sections.title: Visit of Odair Perozin to Loreggia (Padua, Italy)
paragraphs: In 2015, Odair J. Perozin, from Florianópolis, Santa Catarina, informed me that he had visited the place where our ancestors lived in Loreggia, Padua, before immigrating to Brazil.
He visited the Perusin farm, located on Via Morosini, in Loreggia. Odair is a descendant of Antônio Perusin — brother of my 3rd grandfather Pietro Perusin.
There, he was welcomed by Silvio Perusin, also a descendant of Antônio.

After sharing a good wine, as he told me, Silvio, his wife, and son Adriano shared stories about our ancestors and how they all once lived together in the same large house, which still exists today beside Silvio's residence.

image.caption: Photo kindly provided by my cousin Odair. The gathering took place at Silvio Perusin's house, where Silvio, his wife, and his son Adriano Perusin appear together with cousin Odair José Perozin.

Silvio Perusin passed away in 2025.

image.caption: Photo kindly provided by cousin Odair. It shows Silvio, Odair, and the dairy milking machines.

sections.title: Old train station of Adamantina (Adamantina, São Paulo, Brazil, 2023)
paragraphs: On June 9, 2023, our family — my wife, my parents, my brother César, and I — embarked on a journey through time to Adamantina, São Paulo. The goal was to fulfill a deep desire of my father.
To revisit the setting of his childhood. In 1948, at only 6 years old, he accompanied my grandfather and my uncle João in an arduous and memorable work routine.
Every day, they traveled the 5 kilometers that separated the cities of Lucélia and Adamantina to and from the railway tracks, carrying their lunchboxes, tools, and willingness to work.

image.caption: Photo of the old Adamantina train station, belonging to the former Companhia Paulista de Estradas de Ferro, Panorama section.

sections.title: Wooden house built by my grandfather Romeo in 1948 (Adamantina, São Paulo, Brazil, 2023)
paragraphs: My grandfather, a skilled carpenter, had been hired by an English engineer from the Companhia Paulista de Estradas de Ferro to build four wooden houses directly in front of the station.
More than seven decades later, the houses still stand as a testament to his craftsmanship and dedication.

image.alt: Wooden house built by Romeo Perusin
image.caption: Photo of one of the wooden houses built by my grandfather Romeo for the Companhia Paulista de Estradas de Ferro in 1948, in front of the old train station in Adamantina, São Paulo.

sections.title: Photo from our visit to the place (Adamantina, São Paulo, Brazil, 2023)
paragraphs: Seeing my father rediscover those buildings was a moment of immense emotion; for us, it ceased to be only a family story and became a living reality.
It was proof of my grandfather's legacy and effort, immortalized in those wooden planks standing in front of the old station.

image.alt: Family visit to Adamantina train station
image.caption: In this photo: me, my wife, my parents, and my older brother César at the old train station in Adamantina, São Paulo, on June 9, 2023.

sections.title: A reunion after 128 years (Loreggia, Padova, Italy, 2025)
paragraphs: In 2025, a remarkable event occurred: members of my family reunited with relatives in Italy after 128 years of separation.
This reunion symbolized not only the recovery of lost family ties, but also the validation of years of genealogical research.
The meeting brought together different generations and cultures, strengthening the sense of identity and belonging that transcends borders and time.

image.caption: What a beautiful memory! A meeting of generations and surnames that intertwine. Among smiles, we have Luci (my sister), Clodoaldo and Flávio (my nephew), celebrating life alongside Silvano and Marta Scoizzato and many other relatives who make our family's heart beat stronger.

sections.title: An emotional reunion with the Perusin family (Loreggia, Padova, Italy, 2025)
paragraphs: Fate wrote a new chapter in our history: after 130 years of longing and distance, our family finally reunited with our Perusin relatives in Italy.
The setting could not have been more symbolic: the historic Perusin farm, formerly known as Contrada Via Sparella, which once sheltered our ancestors.

image.caption: Photo with Adriano Perusin (son of Silvio, who passed away in 2025), Helio Perusin and his wife, my sister, my brother-in-law, and my nephew.

sections.title: Old mansion where our ancestors lived (Loreggia, Padova, Italy, 2025)
paragraphs: Warmly welcomed by Adriano — son of the late Silvio and descendant of Antonio Perusin, brother of my 3rd grandfather Pietro — our family crossed the threshold of the old mansion where it all began.
Walking through the same rooms from which our immigrant ancestors departed was a plunge into a sea of emotions; a unique experience capable of uniting past and present under the same roof.

image.caption: The old mansion where our ancestors likely lived before immigrating to Brazil, located in the former Contrada Sparella.

sections.title: Interior of the old mansion (Loreggia, Padova, Italy, 2025)
paragraphs: Our family had the privilege of entering the rooms of the mansion where our ancestors once lived. It is thrilling to imagine life inside those walls.

My father remembers stories told by my grandfather Romeo: during harsh winters, the animals were brought indoors so that their shared warmth could help heat the house. A mixture of emotions that deeply connects us to our roots.

image.caption: Interior view of one of the rooms inside the mansion.

sections.title: Interior of the mansion (Loreggia, Padova, Italy, 2025)
paragraphs: Details that tell the story of the past: the interior of this room preserves centuries-old agricultural implements.
Seeing these rustic tools up close helps us reconstruct the history of our family's effort and dedication in Loreggia.

This landscape preserves a 176-year history that began around 1840, when our ancestors left Resana, Treviso, to settle in Loreggia, Padua.
A part of us remains there to this day, honoring the memory of those who, driven by the circumstances of their time, sought a new destiny.

The location is probably the former Contrada Via Sparella, where our ancestors lived before immigrating to Brazil.

sections.title: Scientific Research and DNA Evidence
paragraphs: Modern DNA analysis has reinforced the European origins of the family. Genetic test results indicate a strong presence of Southern and Central European ancestry, with significant Italian and Mediterranean components.
Platforms such as MyHeritage and Genera have helped confirm biological connections between family branches, providing scientific support to historical and genealogical research.

Additional studies involving historical documents, surname distribution, and migration routes suggest possible links between Northern Italy, Austria (Istria and Küstenland), and earlier movements from Central Italy.

image.caption: My DNA data matched the data of Edson Scuciatto, who lives in Curitiba, Paraná, Brazil. This information was obtained through the MyHeritage genealogical platform. Our common ancestors were Giovanni Squizzato and Angela Cucca Dal Broi.

sections.title: Our Family (Brotas, São Paulo, Brazil, 2021)
paragraphs: On March 6, 2021, we celebrated love and resilience as my parents commemorated their 50th wedding anniversary.
On such a memorable occasion, our family gathered together with my mother's relatives to honor this half-century journey.
These were moments of pure gratitude and joy that now remain forever in our memories as a living example of family unity.

sections.title: Our Family (Mauá, São Paulo, Brazil, 2026)
paragraphs: In April 2020, our family gathered with several maternal and paternal relatives to celebrate the birthday of my grandfather Romeo's great-granddaughter.
She is the granddaughter of his youngest son, Carlos Perusin. It was a beautiful celebration, and we spent a wonderful time together as a family.
